lessons.title: Fine-Tune, Prompt, or RAG? The Decision Framework
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The three levers

You have three ways to specialize an LLM: prompting (instructions and few-shot examples in context), RAG (retrieving documents into context), and fine-tuning (updating weights). They solve different problems. Prompting is fastest to iterate and costs nothing to train, but you pay per token forever and behavior is brittle. RAG grounds the model in your documents — the right answer when the problem is knowledge the model lacks. Fine-tuning changes behavior: tone, format, reasoning patterns, tool-use conventions — things that must hold across every response.

## A decision framework

1. **Need the model to know private or fresh facts?** RAG first. Baking facts into weights is expensive, stale-prone, and unreliable — models hallucinate memorized facts.
2. **Need consistent style, format, or a specialized skill** (e.g., always output valid JSON for a tool, follow a domain reasoning pattern)? Fine-tuning wins. A fine-tuned model follows the pattern without a 2,000-token system prompt on every call.
3. **Check the economics.** A heavy system prompt costs tokens on every request. If you serve millions of requests, the one-time GPU cost of fine-tuning plus cheaper inference (shorter prompts, possibly a smaller model) can pay back in weeks. Do the arithmetic for your volume.
4. **Do you have data?** Fine-tuning needs hundreds to thousands of quality examples. No data, no fine-tuning.

## When fine-tuning disappoints

Fine-tuning on 200 examples of company trivia will not make the model reliably recite them — that is a RAG job. Fine-tuning also inherits the base model's weaknesses; it will not fix broken reasoning, and it can degrade general capabilities (catastrophic forgetting) if overdone. Start with the smallest intervention that works: prompt, then RAG, then fine-tune.

## A worked cost example

Make the economics concrete. Suppose your system prompt with few-shot examples is 2,000 tokens and you serve 1M requests a month. At $2.50 per million input tokens, that prompt alone costs $5,000/month — $60k/year — before a single output token. Fine-tuning the same behavior into the model might cost $200-500 in GPU time once, plus lets you shrink the prompt to 200 tokens, cutting the ongoing bill 90%. The breakeven is often weeks, not months, at real volume. The math flips at low volume: 10k requests a month costs $50 in prompt tokens, and no fine-tune pays back. This is why 'it depends on scale' is not a dodge — run your own numbers with your token counts and request volume before choosing.

## Exercise

Take one task you want an LLM to do. Run it through the four questions above and write down your chosen approach plus the one-line reason. If you picked fine-tuning, estimate your example count — if it is under 500, reconsider.

lessons.title: Curating Data for Supervised Fine-Tuning
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Quality beats quantity

The LIMA finding still guides practice: a few thousand excellent examples beat a hundred thousand mediocre ones. Alignment is mostly about teaching format and behavior, and the base model already knows the facts. Budget your effort accordingly: 1,000 to 10,000 carefully reviewed examples is the sweet spot for most SFT projects.

## What good data looks like

Each example should be an instruction (or conversation) paired with a response that exemplifies exactly the behavior you want — tone, structure, thoroughness. Diversity matters more than volume: cover the task distribution, edge cases, and failure modes you care about. Deduplicate aggressively; near-duplicates teach the model to memorize instead of generalize. Filter out low-quality, inconsistent, or unsafe examples — one bad pattern repeated a hundred times becomes model behavior.

## Building the dataset

Sources: human-written seed examples expanded carefully, synthetic generation from a stronger model followed by human verification (never trust raw synthetic output), and real user interactions with expert correction. Format consistently with the chat template your base model expects (e.g., ChatML) — template mismatch at inference is a classic silent bug. Split off a held-out evaluation set before training, and check for contamination: eval examples that leaked into training inflate your metrics and your confidence.

## Diversity and decontamination checklist

Two failure modes dominate SFT datasets: narrowness and leakage. For narrowness, audit your data across axes — task types, input lengths, difficulty, user personas, edge cases — and fill the gaps deliberately. A dataset of 5,000 near-identical customer-support exchanges teaches one trick; 2,000 varied ones teach a skill. For leakage, hash-normalize your eval examples and scan the training set for near-duplicates (embedding similarity above ~0.95 deserves human review). Contaminated evals are worse than no evals because they manufacture confidence. Finally, version your datasets like code: every training run should point at a dataset hash, so when you find a bad example six weeks later, you know exactly which models it touched.

## Verifying synthetic data

When you generate training data with a stronger model, treat its output as a draft, not ground truth. Strong models confidently produce subtly wrong answers, and training on those errors bakes them in. Verify with a pipeline: automatic filters first (format checks, dedup, length bounds), then model-based judging for a second opinion, then human review of a random sample — at least 5% — to calibrate the filters. If the human sample finds more than a few percent bad examples, your filters are too weak. Track the provenance of every example (human, synthetic-verified, synthetic-raw) so you can ablate later and see which source actually helped.

## Exercise

Write 10 gold-standard examples for your task by hand. Then write the 5-point rubric you would use to judge a 50-example batch (correctness, format, tone, diversity, safety). If you cannot judge quality by hand, you cannot curate at scale — fix the rubric first.

lessons.title: SFT Mechanics: The Training Loop, Hyperparameters, and TRL
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## What SFT actually optimizes

Supervised fine-tuning trains the model to predict your response tokens given the instruction — standard next-token cross-entropy, but with the loss masked so it only counts on response tokens, not the prompt. You are not teaching facts; you are teaching the conditional distribution of good responses.

## The TRL way

Hugging Face TRL's SFTTrainer is the standard starting point: it handles chat templates, packing (concatenating short examples to fill the context window for efficiency), and response-only loss masking.

```python
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset('json', data_files='sft_data.jsonl')['train']

args = SFTConfig(
    output_dir='sft-output',
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=8,
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    num_train_epochs=2,
    warmup_ratio=0.05,
    bf16=True,
    packing=True,
    max_seq_length=2048,
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(model='meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct',
                     args=args, train_dataset=dataset)
trainer.train()
```

## Hyperparameters that matter

Learning rate 1e-5 to 2e-4 (smaller for larger models and longer runs); 1 to 3 epochs — more epochs on small data just memorizes; warmup around 5% of steps; weight decay 0.01 to 0.1. Watch eval loss on your held-out set, gradient norms for instability, and sample generations every few hundred steps — numbers lie less when you read the outputs. If train loss keeps falling while eval loss rises, you are overfitting: stop, add data diversity, or lower the learning rate.

## Trade-offs

Full fine-tuning updates every weight — maximum expressiveness, maximum GPU memory (optimizer states dominate). For most teams, parameter-efficient methods (next lesson) get 95% of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

## Reading the curves

Learn to read a training run like a doctor reads vitals. Healthy SFT: train loss falls smoothly, eval loss falls then plateaus, gradient norms stay bounded, and sampled outputs improve steadily. Pathology has signatures: eval loss rising while train loss falls means overfitting — stop early or add data; loss spiking to NaN usually means the learning rate is too high or bf16 overflow — halve the LR and enable gradient clipping; eval loss flat from step one suggests the data is too easy, misformatted, or the model is ignoring it (check your chat template masks correctly). Evaluate every 10-20% of an epoch on a fixed prompt set and read the outputs yourself. Metrics aggregate; reading catches the model that scores well while answering in the wrong language.

## Exercise

Before your first run, write down: expected epochs to convergence, the eval metric that decides 'good enough', and your early-stopping rule. Run, then compare reality to the prediction — the gap is where your intuition grows.

lessons.title: LoRA and QLoRA: Fine-Tuning on a Single GPU
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The LoRA idea

LoRA freezes the base weights W and learns a low-rank update: W + BA, where B and A are small matrices of rank r (typically 8 to 64). With r=16 on a 7B model, trainable parameters drop to well under 1% — yet performance matches full fine-tuning on most tasks. The scaling factor alpha/r controls the update magnitude. Target the attention projections (q_proj, v_proj, and usually k_proj, o_proj) and often the MLP layers for harder tasks.

## QLoRA: adding quantization

QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit NormalFloat, cutting memory roughly 4x versus fp16, and uses paged optimizers to handle memory spikes. The headline result: fine-tuning a 65B model on a single 48GB GPU. The cost is slower training (dequantization overhead) and slight quality loss versus full precision — usually negligible for SFT.

```python
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type='nf4',
                         bnb_4bit_compute_dtype='bfloat16')

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    'meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct', quantization_config=bnb, device_map='auto')

lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                  target_modules=['q_proj', 'k_proj', 'v_proj', 'o_proj'],
                  task_type='CAUSAL_LM')
model = get_peft_model(model, lora)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
```

## Trade-offs

Higher rank helps complex tasks but with diminishing returns past 32 to 64. Merging the adapter into the base weights gives the fastest inference (no adapter overhead) but loses the ability to swap adapters; serving adapters separately (vLLM supports multi-LoRA) lets one base model serve many tasks. Full fine-tuning still wins when you need deep behavioral change across the whole distribution — but try LoRA first; it usually suffices.

## Choosing rank, alpha, and targets

Start with r=16, alpha=32 (alpha = 2x rank is the common convention), targeting all attention projections. This config works surprisingly often and keeps trainable parameters tiny. Raise the rank to 32 or 64 when the task demands substantial new behavior — complex reasoning patterns, new languages, heavy format constraints — but expect diminishing returns past 64 and watch for overfitting on small datasets, where a big rank memorizes. Add the MLP layers (gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj) to targets when attention-only adapters underfit. Variants worth knowing: DoRA decomposes updates into magnitude and direction for slightly better quality at the same rank; LoRA+ uses different learning rates for the A and B matrices to speed convergence. None of these replace the basics: good data and a sensible learning rate matter more than the adapter flavor.

## Exercise

Do the memory math for your target model: parameters x bytes per param (0.5 for 4-bit) + LoRA params + optimizer states on trainable params only. Confirm it fits your GPU before you launch — this one calculation saves more failed runs than any other.

lessons.title: Evaluating, Aligning with DPO, and Serving Your Model
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Evaluate like you mean it

Your held-out set measures task fit, but add broader checks: does the model still reason? Benchmarks like MMLU (knowledge), HumanEval (code), and MT-Bench or AlpacaEval (open-ended quality) catch regressions and catastrophic forgetting. LLM-as-judge evaluations are useful but biased — judges favor their own style and verbosity; calibrate with human spot-checks. Always compare against the base model on the same suite: a fine-tune that gains 5 points on your task but loses 15 on general reasoning needs a second look.

## Alignment basics: DPO

SFT teaches the model what good looks like; preference alignment teaches it to prefer better over worse. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) skips RLHF's reward-model-and-PPO complexity: given pairs of preferred and rejected responses, it directly optimizes the policy to assign higher likelihood to preferred ones. You need preference data — human rankings or a strong model's judgments — and TRL's DPOTrainer runs the same loop as SFT. Keep expectations modest: DPO polishes behavior; it does not create capabilities.

## Serving the fine-tuned model

Merge LoRA adapters into the base model for single-task serving, then quantize (AWQ/GPTQ) for cheaper inference. For multi-tenant setups, vLLM serves one base model with many LoRA adapters attached per request — one GPU, many tasks. Expose via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so existing clients switch with a URL change. Load-test with your real prompt distribution before promising latency numbers.

## Building preference data for DPO

DPO is only as good as its preference pairs. Each training example needs a prompt, a chosen response, and a rejected response — where 'rejected' means worse, not terrible. The most informative pairs are near-misses: two plausible answers where one has a subtle flaw (a wrong fact, a skipped step, a tone violation). Sources that work: human annotators ranking model outputs, a stronger model judging pairs (with human audits for bias), and your own SFT data — the gold response as chosen, an earlier model generation as rejected. You need far fewer pairs than SFT examples; 1,000-5,000 good pairs moves behavior noticeably. Watch for reward hacking in miniature: if rejected responses are always obviously bad, DPO learns a trivial discriminator and behavior barely changes.

## Exercise checklist

Before calling a fine-tune done: beats base model on your task eval; no regression on 2+ general benchmarks; human review of 50+ outputs; preference data collected for DPO if behavior needs polish; serving latency measured under load; rollback to base model is one config change. Ship it.
